bmo-bmo1-2015-02.title: Factorise the difference of squares
bmo-bmo1-2015-02.body:
We have $p^2=b^2-a^2=(b-a)(b+a)$ with $0<b-a<b+a$ (as $a>0$). The only factorisations of $p^2$ into positive integers are $1\cdot p^2$ and $p\cdot p$; the second would need $b-a=b+a$, impossible. Hence
$$b-a=1,\quad b+a=p^2,\qquad\text{so}\qquad a=\frac{p^2-1}{2}.$$

**$12\mid a$.** Since $p$ is odd, $p-1$ and $p+1$ are consecutive even numbers, so one of them is divisible by $4$ and $8\mid (p-1)(p+1)=p^2-1$. Among $p-1,p,p+1$ one is divisible by $3$, and it is not $p$ (a prime $>3$), so $3\mid p^2-1$. Thus $24\mid p^2-1$ and $12\mid a$.

**Perfect square.**
$$2(p+a+1)=2p+(p^2-1)+2=p^2+2p+1=(p+1)^2 .$$ ∎

bmo-bmo1-2015-03.title: Non-adjacent choices on each side
Count one side by a recurrence
bmo-bmo1-2015-03.body:
Let $g_n(k)$ be the number of ways to choose $k$ non-adjacent rooms out of $n$ in a row. Looking at the last room: either it is not chosen ($g_{n-1}(k)$ ways) or it is chosen and the previous room is not ($g_{n-2}(k-1)$ ways). Building the table from $g_0(0)=g_1(0)=1$, $g_1(1)=1$ gives for $n=10$:
$$g_{10}(0..5)=1,\ 10,\ 36,\ 56,\ 35,\ 6 .$$
The number of bookings is $\sum_k g_{10}(k)\,g_{10}(7-k)=36\cdot6+56\cdot35+35\cdot56+6\cdot36=4352$. **Answer: $4352$.**

bmo-bmo1-2015-04.title: A recurrence, then reduce modulo t
bmo-bmo1-2015-04.body:
**Integers.** Put $t_0=x^0+x^0=2$ and $t_1=t$. For $n\ge1$,
$$(x+x^{-1})(x^n+x^{-n})=x^{n+1}+x^{-(n+1)}+x^{n-1}+x^{-(n-1)},$$
so
$$t_{n+1}=t\,t_n-t_{n-1}.$$
Since $t_0,t_1$ are integers and $t$ is an integer, induction shows every $t_n$ is an integer.

**Divisibility.** Reduce the recurrence modulo $t$: $t_{n+1}\equiv -t_{n-1}\pmod t$. With $t_0=2$ and $t_1\equiv0$:
- for odd $n$: $t_n\equiv \pm t_1\equiv 0$;
- for even $n=2m$: $t_{2m}\equiv(-1)^m t_0=\pm2$.

Since $t\ge3$, $t$ does not divide $2$ or $-2$. Hence $t\mid t_n$ if and only if $n$ is odd.

**Answer:** $t$ divides $t_n$ exactly for the odd positive integers $n$. ∎

bmo-bmo1-2015-05.title: Show PQCD is cyclic
bmo-bmo1-2015-05.body:
The points lie on the circle in the order $A,F,B,C,D$. Chord $DF$ separates $A$ from $C$, so it meets segment $AC$: $P$ lies inside segment $AC$ (and on segment $DF$). Similarly chord $CF$ separates $B$ from $D$, so $Q$ lies inside segment $BD$ and segment $CF$.

**Step 1: $P,Q,C,D$ are concyclic.** Since $F$ is the midpoint of arc $AB$, the arcs $AF$ and $FB$ are equal, so the inscribed angles on them are equal:
$$\angle FDB=\angle ACF .$$
As $P$ is on ray $DF$ and $Q$ on ray $DB$, $\angle PDQ=\angle FDB$; as $P$ is on ray $CA$ and $Q$ on ray $CF$, $\angle PCQ=\angle ACF$. So $\angle PDQ=\angle PCQ$. The points $C$ and $D$ lie on the same side of line $PQ$ (both segments $DP$… more simply: $P$ and $Q$ both lie inside the quadrilateral region bounded by $ABCD$ on the side of chord $CD$… and $C,D$ are on the same side of $PQ$ because $PQ$ meets neither segment $CQ$… ), hence $P,Q,C,D$ lie on a circle (converse of angles in the same segment).

**Step 2: the parallel.** In this circle, $\angle QPC=\angle QDC$ (same arc $QC$). Since $Q$ lies on ray $DB$, $\angle QDC=\angle BDC$, and in the original circle $\angle BDC=\angle BAC$ (same arc $BC$). Hence
$$\angle QPC=\angle BAC .$$
$P$ lies on segment $AC$, and $Q$, $B$ lie on the same side of line $AC$, so these are corresponding angles for the lines $PQ$ and $AB$ with transversal $AC$. Therefore $PQ\parallel AB$. ∎

*(With directed angles modulo $180^\circ$ the argument needs no discussion of sides: $\angle(DP,DQ)=\angle(DF,DB)=\angle(CA,CF)=\angle(CP,CQ)$ gives $PQCD$ cyclic, and then $\angle(PQ,PC)=\angle(DQ,DC)=\angle(DB,DC)=\angle(AB,AC)$.)*

bmo-bmo1-2015-06.title: Induction on the multiplier
bmo-bmo1-2015-06.body:
Let $g(n)=1/f(n)$. The condition says $g(a)+g(b)=g(c)$ whenever $\frac1a+\frac1b=\frac1c$.

For positive integers $j,m$ we have the identity
$$\frac{1}{(j+1)m}+\frac{1}{j(j+1)m}=\frac{j+1}{j(j+1)m}=\frac{1}{jm},$$
so
$$g\bigl((j+1)m\bigr)+g\bigl(j(j+1)m\bigr)=g(jm)\qquad\text{for all } j,m\ge1. \tag{$*$}$$

**Claim $P(j)$:** $g(jm)=\dfrac{g(m)}{j}$ for **every** positive integer $m$.

$P(1)$ is trivial. Assume $P(1),\dots,P(j)$. In $(*)$, apply $P(j)$ with $m$ replaced by $(j+1)m$: $g\bigl(j\cdot(j+1)m\bigr)=\dfrac{g((j+1)m)}{j}$. Also $g(jm)=\dfrac{g(m)}{j}$ by $P(j)$. So $(*)$ becomes
$$g\bigl((j+1)m\bigr)\Bigl(1+\frac1j\Bigr)=\frac{g(m)}{j},\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad g\bigl((j+1)m\bigr)=\frac{g(m)}{j+1},$$
which is $P(j+1)$.

Taking $m=1$: $g(n)=g(1)/n$, i.e. $f(n)=n\,f(1)$. Writing $k=f(1)$, a positive integer, $f(n)=kn$.

**Check.** If $f(n)=kn$ and $\frac1a+\frac1b=\frac1c$, then $\frac1{ka}+\frac1{kb}=\frac1k\bigl(\frac1a+\frac1b\bigr)=\frac1{kc}$. ✓

**Answer:** exactly the functions $f(n)=kn$, $k$ a fixed positive integer. ∎
